state.case_summary:
A man in his 60s presented with severe fatigue. His medical history was significant for primary hyperparathyroidism 6 years prior to presentation, for which the patient refused therapeutic management. The patient was cachectic and exhibited significant muscular weakness.

Clinical examination revealed a large tumor on the distal part of the right fourth finger that had gradually enlarged in recent months.

- Laboratory tests:   - Hypercalcemia at 3.6 mmol/L (reference range 2.05-2.55 mmol/L)  - Hypophosphatemia at 0.65 mmol/L (reference range 0.87-1.45 mmol/L)   - Elevated serum parathyroid hormone at 380 pmol/L (reference range 1.6-6.9 pmol/L)- Imaging studies:  - Radiography showed complete lysis of the underlying phalanx and periosteal bone resorption in the phalangeal tuft band  - Chest radiograph revealed important deformation of the ribs  - Thoracic CT scan revealed multiple lesions associated with multiple rib and vertebral fractures  - Skull radiography showed pattern of trabecular resorption with 'salt-and-pepper' appearance  - Cervical ultrasonography revealed a nodule in right thyroid lobe  - Sestamibi parathyroid scintigraphy identified hyperfunctional nodule- Pathology:  Image Title: Histopathology of finger tumor  Image Description: Shows fibrous tissue, woven bone, and supporting vasculature with brown coloration of osteolytic cysts. Numerous giant cells with multiple osteoclastlike nuclei and giant multinucleated cells dispersed in contact with fibers associated with small vessels.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica and brown tumor
B. Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism
C. Parathyroid carcinoma
D. Brown tumor secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism due to parathyroid carcinoma

excluded_candidates: primary malignancy: reason ranked lower due to presence of hyperparathyroidism and characteristic bone lesions
